turns.t: Come in, Mr Gallagher, come in. Terrible weather out there again, isn't it?
Wet, yeah. Soaking.
Did you manage to park all right? The car park's a nightmare on Thursdays.
Eventually. Went round three times.
Ah, you're not the only one. Sit down there, and take your coat off if it's wet.
I'm grand.
Well. It's been a good few weeks since you came out of hospital. How would you say things are going?
Not bad.
Not bad. Tell me a little more about that, if you can.
Walking more. The wife has me out every morning.
Good for her. How far are you getting?
Down to the shop and back. About a mile, maybe.
That's great. And when you're out on that walk, have you had any chest pain at all?
No. None.
What about getting short of breath, going up the hill or the stairs?
No, I'm not.
Any swelling around your ankles in the evenings?
No. Feet are fine.
Lovely. Now let's look at your tablets. Remind me what you're on at the moment.
The aspirin. And the cholesterol one.
The aspirin, is that the 75 mg, once a day?
Yeah. With breakfast.
And the cholesterol tablet, the atorvastatin. Is that 40 mg?
That's it. At night, before bed.
Good. How are you getting on with them, day to day?
Fine. Same as ever.
Do you ever forget a dose, or run short before the repeat comes?
The wife sets them out for me. In a box.
Sensible woman. Keep doing that. Anything you were worried about coming in today?
Just the one thing. Can I go back to the golf?
I'd say yes, in stages. Start with the driving range and a short nine, before you try a full round.
Right. She'll like that, she says I'm under her feet.
Ha. And I should ask, you used to smoke, didn't you? Where are we with that?
Gave up smoking. Twelve years ago now.
Well done. Keep it that way. And you've still got the high blood pressure on your record, from years back.
I do, yeah. They keep an eye on it.
Good. Pop up on the couch there and I'll have a listen to your chest.
Okay.
Breathe in and out through your mouth for me. In... and out. Again.
Your chest is clear, both sides. Nothing to worry about there.
Good.
You can sit up. I won't lie, you look a different man from the one I saw in the ward.
Feel it too.
So, from what I can see today, you're recovering well. That's what I'd call it, a steady recovery, on track.
Good to hear.
I'd like to arrange a blood test for your cholesterol, to check the tablet's doing its job. The nurse at the desk will book it.
Fasting?
No need to fast for this one. Any time of day suits.
Grand.
And I'd like to see you again in six weeks, to go through the result and see how the walking is going.
Six weeks. Right.
Keep the walking up, and build it slowly. Don't push to the point of being wrecked.
I won't. The wife will see to that.
I'm sure she will. Is there anything you'd like to ask me?
Not really.
Nothing at all? Take your time, there's no rush on us.
The car park. Is there a cheaper one?
The one behind the chemist is free after six, but that's no use at this hour. Sorry.
Sure, I'll live.
Then mind yourself out there, Mr Gallagher. Say hello to herself for me.
I will. Thanks, doctor.
Take care now. Mind the wet floor in the corridor.
Will do.

chief_complaint.value: since you came out of hospital

clinical_actions.description: Build walking up slowly and return to golf in stages
